input.said: What does Seth use the Antikythera mechanism to show?

He uses it as an example of an early computer that was analogue, not digital. It is one of the "other games in town" that sit outside Turing-style computation. input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth says the thought experiment fails "at its first hurdle", because it assumes something that can't be done: a perfect silicon replacement for a piece of brain [spya-ahtr6e]. The experiment asks us to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon parts that work in exactly the same way. The supposed conclusion is that cognition and consciousness must be substrate independent, meaning they don't depend on what the system is made of. He notes that Hinton recently used it this way to argue that conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, a property he calls "generative entrenchment". So you can't assume a single neuron can be swapped for a silicon equivalent that keeps its input-output behavior perfectly intact [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste. Replacing them would need an invented silicon metabolism, and he says silicon isn't suited to that [spya-un9fjn].

In the larger argument, this sits inside his first claim, "Brains Are Not Computers". It shows that the software/hardware split doesn't hold in brains, which in turn weakens computational functionalism. That is the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0].

My inference is that his objection targets the premise of the thought experiment, not its logic. If the premise can't be met, the experiment can't support its conclusion. The article doesn't discuss how Chalmers or others might respond, for example by treating the swap as a hypothetical rather than something we could actually build.
